title: Durable execution: workflows that survive crashes
goal: By the end, you can explain how a workflow engine keeps a multi-step order going after the program running it crashes, why each step can still run twice and needs a key, and how to change the code while orders are still in progress.
opening:
Picture ordering a book online. That evening, your banking app shows the money gone. A week later there's no parcel, and the shop's order page still says: Processing.

Behind that page, the shop's program had three jobs: charge your card, set a copy of the book aside in the warehouse, and book a courier. It charged the card. Then its computer restarted for an update, and the program forgot your order halfway through. Nothing will ever come back for the other two jobs.

The tempting fix is to run the order again from the top after a crash. It feels safe, because each step worked the first time. But the first step takes money, and you'd pay twice.

In Calling other services, a key made one call safe to repeat. An order makes three calls, and a crash can land between any two. In this lesson, we'll crash ten thousand orders, write their progress down by hand, then give that job to an engine that replays our code. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The shop's program asks the bank to charge your card, and the bank says yes. Before the program can write that down, its computer restarts. When the program comes back, it finds your order with no charge written down, so it asks the bank to charge the card again. What happens?
options: Nothing bad: the bank notices it charged this card a moment ago and ignores the second request
You're charged twice, unless both requests carry the same key and the bank remembers the first one
Nothing at all: the restart wiped the order, so the program can't ask again
The bank cancels both charges, because they came too close together
warmup.why: The bank can't tell a repeat from a second, honest purchase: people buy two coffees in a row all the time. Only a key that's the same on both requests, as in Calling other services, lets the bank answer the second request with the first charge. The first option is the tempting one, because it's what a person at a till would do. The surprise of this lesson is that even an engine built to survive crashes leaves this gap open, so the key stays.

sections.h: Three calls, and the program can die between any two
sections.body:
An order in the bookshop takes three calls to three systems. Charge the card at the card's bank. Reserve the book in the warehouse, which means setting a copy aside so nobody else gets it. Hand the parcel to the courier. As plain code, it's three lines:

```kotlin
val chargeId = bank.charge(order)
val reservation = warehouse.reserve(order)
courier.ship(order, reservation)
```

Now a deploy, installing a new version of the program, restarts it between the first line and the second. The card is charged and nothing is reserved. Nothing will ever run the second line for this order, either: the only record that the order was halfway done lived in the program's memory, and that's gone. You can't wrap the three calls in one database transaction, a group of changes that a database makes all together or not at all. They go to three systems, and the card's bank takes no part in your database's transactions. (The Transactions track's lesson Atomic commit across machines: two-phase commit and XA shows why few systems offer that.)

Running the whole order again turns every crash after the charge into a second charge. The classic fix is to write progress down, the way a shop worker notes how far they got before the shift ends. A database keeps its data in tables, like spreadsheets. Add a `status` column to the `orders` table, which has one row per order, and update it after each step, in its own small transaction: `NEW`, `CHARGED`, `RESERVED`, `SHIPPED`. A sweeper, a small program that runs by itself every minute, finds orders stuck halfway (not `SHIPPED`, and untouched for five minutes) and carries each one on from its recorded status.

The Try runs 10,000 orders through these strategies. At each of six points, before and after each step's effect, the program dies with probability 0.5%. With no recovery, 247 orders end charged and never shipped. Restarting from the top ships them all, and charges 247 cards twice. The status column cuts that to 50. Those 50 are the crashes that landed after the bank charged but before the `UPDATE`, the database command that records the new status, was saved. That gap never closes, because no transaction in your database can include the bank. Only an idempotency key on the charge brings it to zero: a unique label, here `order-42/charge`, that the bank remembers so it can spot a repeat (Calling other services built one).

So a status column works, with keys, and many payment systems run this way today. The cost shows as such processes multiply. Each one rebuilds the same machinery: a lock so that two sweepers don't take the same order, retries with growing waits, a time limit per step, the keys. A rule such as "refund if the courier hasn't collected within three days" becomes another status, and another query that runs every minute. The process ends up spread over a column, a scheduled program and a piece of code per status. Adding a step means moving every order in progress to a new set of statuses. Brandur Leach's 2017 article on idempotency keys, linked below, builds this approach carefully, with a note of how far the work got after each outside call.

A crash is one way for an order to stop halfway. A firm no is another. Next, we'll see what to do when a step fails for good.

try.title: Crash 10,000 orders four ways
steps: Open `CrashBetweenStepsDemo.kt`. It's plain Kotlin, with no library that saves its progress. Each order runs the three steps, and a seeded random, which gives the same numbers on every run, kills the program at one of six points.
Predict which ways of recovering leave double charges, and how the status column compares with restarting from the top.
From the `labs` folder, run the command below.
Change `CRASH_CHANCE` to `0.02`, run it again, and see which numbers grow.

code.title: CrashBetweenStepsDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
10000 orders; at each of 6 points the process dies with probability 0.005
recovery                    charges charged, unshipped double charges
none                           9959                247              0
restart from top              10255                  0            247
status column                 10051                  0             50
status column and keys        10000                  0              0
```
With `0.02`, the rows read 901 charged and unshipped, 936 double charges for restarting from the top, 200 for the status column, and still 0 with keys. The status column's 50 (or 200) are the crashes between the bank's charge and the `UPDATE` that records it. That's about a fifth of the crashes that come after a charge, because one of the five crash points after the charge lies in that gap. The key closes it, because the bank, not your database, remembers what it already did.

sections.h: When a step fails for good: sagas and compensating steps
sections.body:
A crash is a step that didn't finish. A refusal is different. The warehouse answers that the book is out of stock, and asking again won't change that. By then, the card is charged. You can't roll the charge back the way a database rolls back a transaction, as if it never happened. The money has moved, and the customer may already see it in their banking app. What you can do is take a new action that cancels its effect: a refund.

Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem named this pattern in 1987. A **saga** is a long process split into steps, T1, T2 and so on, each a small transaction of its own. Each step is paired with a compensating step, C1, C2 and so on, that cancels its effect by doing something new. If a step fails for good, the saga runs the compensations of the steps already done, newest first. For the order, a refund cancels the charge, and a release cancels the reservation. If the reservation fails, refund. If the courier refuses the parcel, release the book, then refund. The figure shows the pairs.

Three things about sagas catch people out. First, a compensation is a second action, and the first one stays on the record. The customer's statement shows a charge and a refund, the card network (the company behind the card's brand) may keep a fee, and a confirmation email that went out stays sent. Second, a saga has no isolation, a database's promise that nobody sees a change while it's half done. Between the charge and the refund, anyone can see the order charged but not reserved: the customer, the fraud check (a program that tests whether a payment looks stolen), tonight's reports. Third, a compensation must not fail for good. A refund that can't go through becomes a job for the support team. So compensations are retried until they succeed, and they need idempotency keys as much as the forward steps do.

So order the steps so that whatever is hardest to undo comes last. Releasing a reservation is cheap, and nobody outside sees it. A refund is visible. A parcel in a courier's van can't be undone by any program. So `ship` goes last.

**Put the step you can't undo last. Nothing after it may fail.**

Where does a saga keep track of which steps are done and which compensations are due? In the hand-built version, in the status column again, with extra statuses for each compensation. Next, we'll move that bookkeeping into an engine.

sections.h: Durable execution: write down every step, then replay the code
sections.body:
Durable execution keeps the three-line program and makes it survive the crash. (Durable means it lasts through a crash.) It splits the program in two. **Activities** do the work that touches the outside world: `charge`, `reserve`, `ship`. They're ordinary code, and they may fail and be retried. The **workflow** is the code that decides what happens next, with its `if`s, loops, waits and compensations. It never touches the outside world itself.

Temporal is one well-known engine that works this way: a free program that runs workflows and keeps a record of each one, with libraries for Java, Go and other languages. A Temporal server (version 1.32 in November 2026) is a few programs with a database of their own. It keeps an **event history** for every run of a workflow. The history is append-only: entries are only ever added at the end. Workers are your programs. They run the workflow and activity code, and keep asking the server for tasks.

When a worker runs the workflow code and reaches `activities.charge(...)`, Temporal's library, the part of Temporal inside your program, doesn't call the bank. It sends the server a command: schedule the activity `Charge`. The server adds `ActivityTaskScheduled` to the history and hands the task to an activity worker, which calls the bank and reports back. The server adds `ActivityTaskCompleted`, with the charge's ID, and the workflow code carries on with that value. `Workflow.sleep(Duration.ofHours(24))` becomes a timer: the server records `TimerStarted`, and no thread, no path of work in your program, waits for a day.

Now kill the worker while the order sleeps. The history is safe in the server. A day later, the timer fires, and another worker gets the task. It has never seen this order, so it **replays** it: it runs the workflow function from the first line, against the history. When the code reaches `charge`, the library finds the completed event and returns the recorded charge ID at once, without calling the bank. The same happens for `reserve`, and the sleep returns because its timer has already fired. Then the code reaches `ship`, which has no event yet, so this time the library schedules it for real.

Picture an instruction sheet and a notebook, handed from one shop worker to the next at a change of shift. The first worker writes each finished step in the notebook: "10:02, charged the card, receipt ch_1." The next worker reads the sheet from the top with the notebook open, skips every step it shows, uses the results written there, and starts work at the first step with no entry. The sheet is the workflow code, the notebook is the event history, and each line in it is an event.

Databases survive crashes the same way. They write each change to a log, a file that's only ever added to, and after a crash they read it back from the start (Write-ahead logging and crash recovery, in the Storage engines track). Here, the log holds a program's steps.

A healthy worker rarely replays. It keeps recent workflows in memory, and the server sends a workflow's next task back to the same worker, which Temporal calls sticky execution. If that worker has died, any worker gets the task after a short wait, 5 seconds by default in the Java library. Look closely, though, at the moment between the bank's answer and the event that records it. Next, we'll crash right there.

try.title: Kill a worker in the middle of an order
steps: Open `KillWorkerDemo.kt` and the shared `DemoOrders.kt`. The demo runs Temporal's test server inside the JVM, the program that runs Java and Kotlin code, using the `temporal-testing` library, so there's nothing to install. Its workers turn sticky execution off, because this test server never takes a task back from a dead worker the way a real server does.
Predict which worker charges the card, and which worker runs `ship`.

code.title: KillWorkerDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.enc.l05.demo

/**
 * Starts an order on worker-1, kills worker-1 while the order waits 24 hours for the courier,
 * then starts worker-2, which finishes the order from the history alone.
 */
fun main() {
    quiet()
    newEnv().use { env ->
        val client = env.workflowClient
        val bank = FakeBank(honorKeys = true)
        val first = startWorker(client, "worker-1", OrderV1::class.java, StepsImpl(bank))
        val order = startOrder(client, "order-42")
        waitForTimer(client, "order-42")
        first.kill()
        println("worker-1 killed while order-42 sleeps; it ran charge=${first.steps.runs("charge")} reserve=${first.steps.runs("reserve")}")

        val second = startWorker(client, "worker-2", OrderV1::class.java, StepsImpl(bank))
        println("result: ${order.getResult(String::class.java)}") // the test server skips the 24 hours
        println("worker-2 ran charge=${second.steps.runs("charge")} reserve=${second.steps.runs("reserve")} ship=${second.steps.runs("ship")}")
        println("cards charged: ${bank.charges.get()}")
        println()
        println("the event history of order-42:")
        client.fetchHistory("order-42").events.forEach { println(describe(it)) }
        second.kill()
    }
}

the event history of order-42:

  4  WORKFLOW_TASK_COMPLETED

  7  ACTIVITY_TASK_COMPLETED
  ...

(Events 8 to 16, the reservation and the timer's workflow tasks, are trimmed.) Worker-2 never called the bank or the warehouse. In the workflow task of events 19 to 21, it replayed the code from the first line against events 1 to 18, got `ch_1` and `res_1` from the history, and sent one new command: schedule `Ship`. The test server skipped the 24 hours, so the demo takes about 2 seconds.

aside.title: Doesn't replaying from the first line get slow?
aside.body: Less than you'd think. A replayed step calls nothing: it reads its result from the history, so replay costs a little computing, not a trip to the bank. And as the section says, a healthy worker rarely replays at all. The history does have a limit: 51,200 events or 50 MB for one run, with warnings from 10,240 events or 10 MB. A workflow that loops for years, such as a monthly subscription, uses continue-as-new: it closes its run and starts a fresh one with the same ID, carrying its state over, so each history stays short.

sections.h: Exactly once means written down once, so each step still needs a key
sections.body:
Go back to the moment between the bank's answer and the `ActivityTaskCompleted` event. Say the activity worker charged the card and died before it could report back. The server knows only that an attempt started and never finished. After the activity's start-to-close timeout, the longest one attempt may take, it schedules another attempt, and the card is charged again. No engine can close this gap, for the same reason the status column couldn't: the bank's change and the engine's record of it are two writes in two systems.

The shift notebook breaks right here. A worker who charged the card but hadn't written it down yet leaves no trace, so the next worker charges again. A person might glance at the till and notice; the engine sees only the notebook.

So activities run **at least once**. Temporal's default retry policy, its rules for trying an activity again, never gives up: it waits 1 second, then doubles the wait each time, up to 100 seconds between attempts. (Workflows themselves don't retry by default.) Temporal's own docs ask you to make activities idempotent, safe to run twice, and the engine makes that easy. The workflow ID, the name of one run, stays the same for the run's whole life, and each activity's input is recorded once. So a key built from them, `"$workflowId/charge"`, is the same on every retry and every replay. Pass it to the bank, and the bank turns the second attempt into a replay of the first. In the Try, the charge activity runs twice either way. The card is charged twice without the key, and once with it.

That's what "exactly once" means in these engines: the workflow's progress, its decisions and recorded results, is applied once. Other engines keep that record in other places. Two of them come from AWS, Amazon's cloud, which rents out computers and ready-made programs by the hour:

| Engine (November 2026) | What it is | Where progress is written | How it resumes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Temporal (server 1.32, Java library 1.40) | a server that workers ask for tasks | an event history in the Temporal server | replays the code against the history |
| Restate (1.8, Java and Kotlin library 2.11) | a server in front of your programs that calls them | a journal for each call, in the Restate server | replays, skipping finished steps |
| DBOS Transact (Java 1.2) | a library inside your program, with no extra server | rows of saved progress in your own PostgreSQL, a free database | reruns, returning saved results |
| AWS Step Functions, Standard | Amazon's workflow service; you write the steps in JSON, a text format | the history of each run | moves to the next step; no replay |
| AWS Lambda durable functions (since December 2025) | Amazon's pay-per-call functions, with saved progress | checkpoints written by its library | reruns from the start, skipping saved steps |

Each one qualifies the claim. Restate says each call of a function runs exactly once, whatever fails. Yet by the argument above, a side effect inside a step can still repeat if the crash comes before the step's result reaches the journal. DBOS says its steps are tried at least once and never run again once they complete. Step Functions Standard is exactly once unless you configure `Retry`, and its Express type is at least once (when the caller doesn't wait) or at most once (when it does). So read every exactly-once claim as effectively once: at-least-once execution, plus duplicates removed by key. The Messaging track meets the same claim in its lesson Transactions and exactly-once.

**Every step can run twice. Give every outside call a key.**

Replay has one more condition, and it bites on the day you change the code. Next, we'll break it.

try.title: A charge that runs twice
steps: Open `AtLeastOnceDemo.kt`. `StepsImpl`, in `DemoOrders.kt`, charges the bank. Then, on the first attempt only, it throws an exception, as if the worker had died before reporting back.
Predict, for a bank that ignores keys and for one that honours them, how often the charge activity runs and how often the card is charged.

code.title: AtLeastOnceDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
bank honours keys=false: SHIPPED, charge activity ran 2x, card charged 2x
      5  ACTIVITY_TASK_SCHEDULED      Charge
      6  ACTIVITY_TASK_STARTED        attempt 2 on worker-1
      7  ACTIVITY_TASK_COMPLETED
bank honours keys=true: SHIPPED, charge activity ran 2x, card charged 1x
```
The workflow sees one charge either way: one scheduled event, one completed event. The failed first attempt left no event of its own. The server retried inside the activity and wrote down only the attempt that finished, attempt 2. The bank, though, saw two requests. Only the key `order-7/charge`, the same on both attempts, let it answer the second with the first charge.

sections.h: Changing the code while orders are still running
sections.body:
Replay has one condition. Given the same history, the workflow code must make the same decisions in the same order: it must be deterministic. So workflow code may not use anything that can differ between runs: `Random`, `UUID.randomUUID()`, the system clock, `Thread.sleep`, threads of its own, files or network calls. The library has safe versions, `Workflow.randomUUID()`, `Workflow.currentTimeMillis()` and `Workflow.sleep(...)`, whose values come from the history on replay. Everything else belongs in activities. Temporal's checker, Workflow Check, reads your code without running it and catches many slips.

The harder case is your own deploy. Version 1 of the order workflow is charge, reserve, sleep, ship, and 40,000 orders are asleep in their 24-hour wait. Version 2 adds the fraud check before the charge. When a version-1 order wakes up on a version-2 worker, the worker replays it. The new code's first command is "schedule `CheckFraud`", but the history says the first activity was `Charge`. The library stops with a `NonDeterministicException`. Temporal counts it as a failed workflow task, one failed turn of running the workflow code, and retries it, so the order stays open and stuck until you deploy code that matches its history. In the notebook picture, the next worker got an edited instruction sheet, and the notebook no longer lines up with it.

There are two ways out. Patching keeps one path for each kind of history:

```kotlin
val version = Workflow.getVersion("fraud-check", Workflow.DEFAULT_VERSION, 1)
if (version >= 1 && !activities.checkFraud(orderId, amountCents)) return "REJECTED"
```

The first time a run reaches `getVersion` for real, the library records a marker in the history with the newest version, 1. A version-1 history has no marker, so on replay `getVersion` returns `DEFAULT_VERSION` (-1), and the old path runs. When no older runs are left, delete the old branch, but keep `getVersion("fraud-check", 1, 1)` for a while before you remove it too. The other way out is never to replay old histories on new code. Temporal's Worker Versioning, released for everyone in 2026, can pin each run to, meaning keep it on, the version of the code it started on. Restate treats every deployed version as fixed, and calls in progress finish on the version they started on. Either way, before you deploy, replay saved real histories against the new code with `WorkflowReplayer`, Temporal's tool for exactly that.

Even a compiler, the program that turns your source code into code the JVM can run, can break replay. Kotlin 2.4 compiles a method reference such as `activities::charge` (a way to pass a function without calling it) differently from Kotlin 2.2. Temporal's Java library up to 1.40 doesn't recognize the new form when you pass it to `Async.function` or `Async.procedure`, helpers that start an activity without waiting for it. So it runs the call on a new workflow thread, which can change the order of commands. Workflows started under Kotlin 2.2 then fail with `NonDeterministicException` when they replay on code built with 2.4, with no change to the source at all. The fix reached the library's newest, not yet released code in October 2026, after 1.40.0. The labs build with Kotlin 2.4.21 on 1.40, so their workflow code calls activities directly.

Every engine in this lesson trusts one thing completely: the database that holds its histories. If the machine under that database dies, the histories die with it, unless copies of the data live on other machines. Keeping such copies in step is where the next part of the course begins.

steps: Open `ReplayDemo.kt` and the three workflow classes in `DemoOrders.kt`: `OrderV1`, `OrderV2Naive` (the fraud check added in front of the charge) and `OrderV2` (the same change behind `getVersion`).
Predict which replay fails, and at which event.

code.title: ReplayDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
a version-1 history with 28 events
OrderV2Naive: io.temporal.worker.NonDeterministicException: [TMPRL1100] Failure handling event 5 of type 'EVENT_TYPE_ACTIVITY_TASK_SCHEDULED' during replay. [TMPRL1100] Command COMMAND_TYPE_SCHEDULE_ACTIVITY_TASK doesn't match event EVENT_TYPE_ACTIVITY_TASK_SCHEDULED with EventId=5 on check activityType with an expected value 'name: "CheckFraud"' and an actual value 'name: "Charge"'.
OrderV2: replays cleanly
```
Event 5 is the first scheduled activity. The naive version wanted to schedule `CheckFraud` there, and the history says `Charge`. The patched version asks `getVersion`, finds no marker, takes the old path and matches every event. `WorkflowReplayer` is what a CI job runs, before a deploy, over histories saved from real orders (fetched with `WorkflowClient.fetchHistory`).

compare.title: The same order, hand-built and as a Temporal workflow

a.label: Status column and sweeper
a.title: runs every minute

b.label: Temporal workflow
b.title: replayed after any crash

compare.note: Both versions write progress down, and both need a key on every outside call. The difference is where the process lives. On the left, it's spread over a status column, a query that runs every minute, a lock and a branch per status. (`SKIP LOCKED` lets each sweeper take only rows that no other sweeper holds; the Transactions track's lesson Lost updates: row locks, SKIP LOCKED and job queues covers it.) The wait for the courier is a condition checked every minute, and a new step means new statuses. On the right, the process is ordinary code, read from top to bottom, and the engine supplies the history, the retries, the timers and the move to another worker after a crash. The price on the right is determinism: that function must replay the same way, so changing it needs `getVersion` or pinned versions.

worked.title: Start one workflow per Kafka event, even when the event arrives twice

steps.say: A small program reads "order placed" events from Kafka, a program that keeps a log of messages for other programs to read, and starts an order workflow for each one. Kafka can deliver an event twice, for example when the reading program crashes before it records how far it got (the Messaging track covers when). The workflow ID is your duplicate check, so build it from the order ID, never from a random UUID.
steps.code:
val options = WorkflowOptions.newBuilder()
    .setWorkflowId("order-$orderId")   // the business key
    .setTaskQueue("orders")
    .setWorkflowIdReusePolicy(WorkflowIdReusePolicy.WORKFLOW_ID_REUSE_POLICY_REJECT_DUPLICATE)
    .build()

steps.say: Start the run. While a run with that ID is open, a second start throws `WorkflowExecutionAlreadyStarted`. That's the duplicate delivery, so mark the event as handled and move on.

Mind the reuse policy. By default (`ALLOW_DUPLICATE`), once the first run has closed, the same ID may start a new run, so an event delivered again after the order finished would start the order again. `REJECT_DUPLICATE` keeps the ID taken for as long as the closed run's history is kept. `StartOnceDemo.kt` runs both deliveries and a late third one; with the default policy, the third line prints `true`.
steps.code:
$ ./gradlew :flow:demo -Pmain=sfz.enc.l05.demo.StartOnceDemoKt --console=plain -q
first delivery started a run:  true
second delivery started a run: false
after the run closed, a third:  false
cards charged: 1

lab.title: An order workflow that survives a dead worker and a deploy
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the tests once. All 10 fail within seconds, because the stub's `TODO` fails every workflow. They use temporal-testing's test server inside the JVM: no Docker, no Temporal command-line tool, and the 24-hour wait is skipped.

Read `OrderApi.kt` (the interfaces), `OrderActivitiesImpl.kt` (finished activities that count their runs and can fail right after their effect) and `World.kt` (the pretend bank, warehouse and courier).

In `OrderWorkflowImpl.kt`, write `process` the way version 1 had it: charge, reserve, `Workflow.sleep(PICKUP_WAIT)`, ship. Pass each activity a key built from `Workflow.getInfo().workflowId` and the step's name.
Add the compensations. Catch `ActivityFailure` around `reserve` (refund, then return "REFUNDED") and around `ship` (release, refund, then return "CANCELLED").

Add the fraud check at the top, behind `Workflow.getVersion(FRAUD_CHECK_CHANGE, Workflow.DEFAULT_VERSION, 1)`. Run all 10 tests. `CrashAndUpgradeTest` stops a worker in the middle of an order, and wakes up a run started on `OrderWorkflowV1` (in the test folder) on your code.

Break it on purpose: replace the `getVersion` call with `val version = 1`, and run `./gradlew :flow:test --tests 'sfz.enc.l05.CrashAndUpgradeTest'`. Three tests fail: two with a `NonDeterministicException` at event 5, and one because your history no longer has a version marker. Put the call back.
hints: An activity that fails for good reaches workflow code as `io.temporal.failure.ActivityFailure`. Catch that, not `ApplicationFailure`, which is its cause.
Keys like `"$id/charge"`, with `val id = Workflow.getInfo().workflowId`, are the same on every retry and replay. `java.util.UUID.randomUUID()` in workflow code would give a different value on replay.

If the version-1 tests fail with a `NonDeterministicException`, either the fraud check runs before `getVersion` has answered, or your old path doesn't send the same commands as `OrderWorkflowV1`, in the same order.

The test setup makes a `TODO` or a determinism error fail the workflow at once (`setFailWorkflowExceptionTypes` in `OrderHarness.kt`). In production, both only fail the workflow task, which Temporal retries until you deploy a fix.

drill.title: Write a patch from memory
drill.prompt: The order workflow with the fraud check is running in production. The next version must send a receipt, with an activity `sendReceipt(key, orderId)`, right after `ship`. It mustn't break runs that are asleep before `ship`, or runs whose history already goes past it. Write the lines from `ship` to `return`. Then compare. Which versions did you pass to `getVersion`, and where does the key come from?

recap: An order that calls several systems can stop between any two calls, and no database transaction can include a card's bank. Running it again from the top charges twice.
A status column and a sweeper carry orders on after a crash, with keys. But every process rebuilds the locks, retries, timers and keys, and its logic ends up spread over a column and a scheduled job.

A saga pairs each step with a compensating step and, when a step fails for good, runs the compensations of the finished steps, newest first. Both actions stay on the record, others can see the state in between, and compensations are retried until they succeed.

Durable execution writes each step's result to a durable history (Temporal's event history, Restate's journal, DBOS's rows in PostgreSQL). After a crash, a worker replays the code and skips every step already recorded.
"Exactly once" means the workflow's progress is recorded once. Activities run at least once, so every outside call needs a key built from the workflow ID and the step.

The limit: workflow code must replay the same way every time, and even a compiler upgrade can break that. Change it with `Workflow.getVersion` or pinned versions, and test it against real histories with `WorkflowReplayer` before you deploy.
closing:
We started with an order that charged a card and then forgot the rest. A status column can carry such an order on, and a workflow engine does it by writing down every step and replaying the code. Neither can stop a step from running twice, so every outside call still carries a key.

Open an order page in a shop's app or website. The list it shows, such as paid, packed and shipped, is a history written one step at a time. Find the step that can't be undone.

Next, in the Replication track, which opens Part III, Data across machines, we'll keep copies of one database on several machines, and ask how the copies stay in step.

quiz.q: A Temporal worker is killed while a workflow waits in `Workflow.sleep(Duration.ofDays(3))`. What happens to the wait?
options: It's lost; someone must start the workflow again
The next worker starts the 3-day wait again from zero
The workflow fails with a timeout
It lives in the server as a timer; when it fires, any worker replays the workflow and carries on
quiz.why: The sleep became a `TimerStarted` event, so the server owns the timer. When it fires, a worker replays the history, in which the timer has fired, and carries on. Nothing starts the wait again. The second option would be true of `Thread.sleep`, which keeps the wait only in one thread's memory and has no place in workflow code.

quiz.q: Which line is safe inside a Temporal workflow method?
options: `if (Random.nextInt(100) < 5) activities.checkFraud(orderId, cents)`
`val key = Workflow.getInfo().workflowId + "/charge"`
`val now = System.currentTimeMillis()`
`Thread.sleep(1_000)` to wait before a retry
quiz.why: The workflow ID comes from the history, so it's the same on every replay. A random number or the system clock can differ on replay and change which commands the code sends. `Thread.sleep` blocks a thread without recording anything. Use `Workflow.sleep`, `Workflow.currentTimeMillis` or `Workflow.newRandom` instead.

quiz.q: An activity calls the bank's `POST /charges`, which honours an `Idempotency-Key`. Which key stops a retried activity from charging twice?
options: `"$workflowId/charge"`, built in the workflow and passed in, the same on every attempt and replay
A UUID made inside the activity on each attempt
The activity's attempt number
None is needed, because Temporal promises exactly once
quiz.why: As in Calling other services, a key must be made once per operation and sent with every attempt. A UUID made inside the activity is new on every attempt, which is exactly the "new key each time" client that charged 313 cards twice. Temporal records the workflow's progress once, but the activity's code runs at least once.

quiz.q: You add a new activity before `charge` and deploy without `getVersion`. Runs started on the old code wake up on the new workers. What happens by default?
options: They run the new activity and carry on normally
Temporal keeps them on the old code automatically
Replay raises a `NonDeterministicException`; the workflow task fails and is retried, so the runs stay open and stuck until a matching deploy
They're marked failed, and their compensations run
quiz.why: Replay compares the new code's first command (schedule the new activity) with the history (schedule `Charge`) and stops. By default, that fails only the workflow task, which Temporal retries. Nothing is lost, but nothing moves. Keeping old runs on old code is what Worker Versioning does, but only if you deploy that way.

quiz.q: Amazon's AWS Step Functions describes its Standard workflows as exactly once. When can a step's work run more than once?
options: Never; that's what exactly once means
Only in Express workflows
Only when you publish a new version of the workflow
When the step has a `Retry` set: a failed attempt runs again, so the step must be idempotent
quiz.why: AWS's own table qualifies it: exactly once unless you set `Retry`. A task that did its work and then failed or timed out is run again. Express workflows are at least once or at most once by design, so the second option is true of them, but it isn't the only case.

flashcards.front: In Temporal, what's the difference between a workflow and an activity?
flashcards.back: The workflow is code that decides what happens next, and it's replayed after a crash, so it must be deterministic. An activity does the outside work, such as a charge, and may be retried.

flashcards.front: What does Temporal write down when workflow code calls an activity?
flashcards.back: `ActivityTaskScheduled`, then `ActivityTaskStarted` and `ActivityTaskCompleted` with the result, in the run's event history.

flashcards.front: Why do Temporal activities run at least once?
flashcards.back: A worker can do the work and die before reporting it. The server sees an unfinished attempt and retries it after the timeout.

flashcards.front: What does `Workflow.getVersion(id, DEFAULT_VERSION, 1)` return when replaying a history recorded before the change?
flashcards.back: `Workflow.DEFAULT_VERSION`, which is -1. A run that reaches it for real records a marker with version 1.
A long process split into steps, each with a compensating step. When a step fails for good, the compensations of the finished steps run, newest first. Others can see the state in between.

flashcards.front: What did Kotlin 2.4 change for Temporal's Java library up to 1.40?
flashcards.back: Method references passed to `Async.function` or `Async.procedure` compile to a form the library doesn't recognize, so it runs them on a new workflow thread. That can break the replay of runs started under Kotlin 2.2.

flashcards.front: How large can one Temporal workflow history get?
flashcards.back: 51,200 events or 50 MB, with warnings from 10,240 events or 10 MB. Long loops use continue-as-new to start a fresh history.

terms.plain: Running ordinary code so that every step's result is written down safely, and the code can carry on after a crash by replaying against that record.
The code that decides the steps of a process and their order. The engine can replay it at any time, so it must make the same decisions every time.
One step that touches the outside world, such as a charge or an email. It runs at least once and may be retried.
Temporal's record of one workflow run, only ever added to: activities scheduled and completed, timers started and fired, version markers.
Running the workflow code from the start against its history, returning recorded results instead of repeating finished steps.
Making the same decisions every time it runs on the same input. Workflow code must be, or replay goes wrong.
A process split into steps, each with a compensating step that cancels its effect, run newest first when a later step fails for good.
A new action that cancels an earlier step's effect, such as a refund for a charge. Both actions stay on the record.

explain_back.prompt: A friend who is moving a shop's payment code onto Temporal says: "Once we're on Temporal, we can drop the idempotency keys. Temporal gives us exactly once." Explain what Temporal promises and what it doesn't.
explain_back.answer: Temporal promises that the workflow's progress is kept safe and applied once. Every activity's result goes into the event history, and after a crash any worker replays the workflow code against that history. Steps that are already recorded return their saved results, so the order never forgets where it was and never decides a finished step again. Temporal doesn't promise that an activity's effect happens once. A worker can charge the card and die before it reports success. The server then sees an unfinished attempt and retries it, and the bank sees a second request. Activities run at least once by design. So the keys stay: build one per step from the workflow ID ("$workflowId/charge"), which is the same on every retry and replay, and make the bank or your own records ignore repeats of it. Exactly once for the business is at-least-once execution plus duplicates removed by key.

deeper.body:
A workflow can take input while it runs. In Temporal, a signal is a message sent into a running workflow ("the courier collected the parcel"), a query reads its state without adding to the history, and an update is a checked change that waits for an answer and is recorded once accepted. A step that waits for a person to approve something is a workflow waiting for a signal, possibly for days, at no cost.

The Java library has a `Saga` helper class that collects compensations and runs them in reverse order. Its `addCompensation` takes a function, and from Kotlin that tempts you to write `saga.addCompensation(activities::refund, key, chargeId)`. Given the Kotlin 2.4 issue of the last section, pass a lambda instead, `saga.addCompensation { activities.refund(key, chargeId) }`, which behaves the same under every compiler version.

Temporal has no Kotlin library of its own yet. From Kotlin you use the Java library, 1.40, with its `temporal-kotlin` add-on, which adds shortcuts such as `ActivityOptions { ... }`. Restate, by contrast, ships a Kotlin library of its own.

The idea is older than any of these engines. Microsoft's Durable Functions and Uber's Cadence, built by the engineers who went on to found Temporal, use the same history-and-replay model. For the book's view of workflows, durable execution and its determinism caveats, see Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 5. The book returns to determinism in chapter 9, on the trouble with distributed systems.
